Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

At a closing: Where a federally regulated lender must require it, the legal minimum is the loan balance or the NFIP's limit for the property, whichever is less (42 U.S.C. §4012a(b)). If such a lender notifies you that coverage is needed and you do not buy it within 45 days, the lender must buy it for you and can charge you for it (42 U.S.C. §4012a(e)). If you think a lender's high-risk-zone finding is wrong, you and the lender together can ask FEMA to review it within 45 days of the lender's notice; a fee applies (44 CFR §65.17). Buying a home with an NFIP policy: the seller can assign the policy to you in writing when title transfers, and FEMA says a below-full-risk discount can move to the new owner that way.

45.7% of Kings County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 45.7% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 27.4% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $1,088 a year ($91 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $722 and $1,370. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $722 · Typical $1,088 · A quarter pay over $1,370 · A tenth pay $1,923 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 3,759 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $4.5 billion of building and $726.5 million of contents coverage across all Kings County policies.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Congress has to keep renewing the NFIP's authority. During a lapse, NFIP policies cannot be bought, renewed or increased until the authority returns. Policies already in force run to their expiration date and claims on them are still handled, though FEMA says the money to pay claims may be limited.

What it won't pay: The policy generally counts a flood only when water covers two or more acres of normally dry land or two or more properties, one of them yours. A standard NFIP home policy does not pay for a hotel or other living costs while you are out of the home, or for belongings outside the building, and it limits what it pays for in a basement. Belongings are paid at actual cash value (their used value), not the cost of new ones.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood.

NFIP claim denied? You can appeal to FEMA within 60 days of the date on the denial letter, and you can sue within one year of the denial. An appeal does not extend that year. If repairs would cost 50 percent or more of the building's market value before the flood, it counts as substantially damaged under federal rules, and local floodplain rules can require elevating or other work. On an NFIP policy with building coverage, Increased Cost of Compliance pays up to $30,000 toward that; the local official's letter has to come before the work starts.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, law.cornell.edu, agents.floodsmart.gov, ecfr.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 6,319 NFIP flood claims and $327.6 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2012, 2021 and 2023.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2012 ($304,684,259), 2021 ($6,527,978), 2023 ($3,849,332). Total paid $327,630,683. Totals for the latest two years are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

That is 6,319 claims since 1978 against 18,764 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 31, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 63.7% of the 2,487 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 2,487 policies reporting one)63.7%New York: 53.6%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)88.5%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 4,945 claims paid with a damage figure)5.3%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 31, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

35.8% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $861, full-risk $942 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$861
  • Median full-risk premium$942
  • Pay below full-risk35.8% of 3,759New York: 49.9%

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

A renewal paid after the 30-day grace period leaves a lapse in coverage, and FEMA says a lapse may affect a policy's statutory discounts (what keeps a bill below full risk).

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 31, 2026.

Can I pay less?

The usual building deductible here is $2,000 (54.6% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways to lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

Does my town get a community discount?

Not through a community discount: none of Kings County's 0 NFIP communities has one.

The Community Rating System cuts NFIP premiums in communities that do extra flood work. A community named for the county covers its unincorporated area only.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Community Status Book (CRS). Data: FEMA's current Community Status Book; retrieved October 31, 2026.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for coastal flooding and Very High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Very High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience; it is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $2.7 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: coastal flood loss here is higher than in about 53% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $181.2 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: inland flood loss here is higher than in about 9% of U.S. counties. Loss figures model all flood loss, insured or not, so they run far above insurance payouts. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 31, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $191.4 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $5,596 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 31, 2026.
